media.description: One half of a stereograph card showing the Eiffel Tower and the Champ de Mars from the Trocadéro, used as broad Paris context for Kaper’s 1933–34 period.
media.altText: Half of a stereograph card: the Eiffel Tower and Champ de Mars seen past a bronze eagle on the Trocadéro terrace.
media.rightsNote: The card prints its own number and title, “3190 Champ de Mars and the Eiffel Tower from the Trocadero Palace, Paris, France”, and the Library of Congress catalogues it under LCCN 2004674653 as a Keystone View Company stereograph of about 1931. That settles the part PICRYL could not: it is a United States work, so the URAA, which restored copyright only in foreign works, does not reach it, and the question is the United States one of renewal. A work published in 1931 whose copyright was not renewed has been in the public domain since 1960; one that was renewed runs ninety-five years, to 1 January 2027. The Library of Congress catalogue entry states the position and could not be opened from here, so the renewal is recorded as unconfirmed rather than asserted.

timelineEvents.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
timelineEvents.label: 1933 · Berlin–Vienna–Paris migration
timelineEvents.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
timelineEvents.longDescription: In 1933, after UFA terminated the contracts of its Jewish employees, Kaper and Jurmann left Berlin and, by way of Vienna, settled in Paris. His route ran through Vienna, where he had supervised the French version of Abenteuer am Lido, and the departure itself falls between the spring and the summer of 1933. Kaper’s oral history returns twice to an attack on him and his wife by a group of Nazis in a Berlin street, once within a story about self-defence and once as an aside to his account of film work, where he set it apart from his music. The attack does not explain his music, but it marks the point at which working conditions in the German film industry could no longer be separated from questions of safety.
